#4341. Bentley’s First EV Is Already Sold Out, And Production Hasn’t Even Started

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Bentley’s first electric car, the Torcal SUV, looks like a hit already. Even though production hasn’t started yet, the $220,000+ EV is sold out for 2027, according to Frank-Steffen Wallier, the company’s head honcho, quoted by Automotive News.

The British luxury automaker said that all available production slots for next year have already been allocated and that the company is now taking orders that will be delivered in 2028. Bentley didn’t say how many EVs it will build in 2027, but the initial customer response has made the marque quite happy with the outcome.

“Needless to say, we’re very pleased with the response and position we’re in,” a company spokesperson told Automotive News.

That’s great news for Bentley, which isn’t doing great in terms of sales and profit. From January through September, it sold 5,970 cars globally, 17% fewer compared to the same period last year. Meanwhile, the profit dropped by more than half to $54.1 million through the first nine months of the year.

The Torcal, which is smaller than the Bentayga SUV, is the brand’s cheapest model, though it still costs a pretty penny. The base Torcal starts at $222,495, followed by the more powerful Torcal S at $262,695, and the Torcal First Edition at $300,995. All things considered, Walliser said that the smaller size and relatively lower price compared to the Bentayga have attracted new and younger customers to the brand.

By comparison, the Bentayga starts at $231,150, the Flying Spur sedan starts at $254,850, and the Continental GT two-door starts at $288,750.

So far, the Torcal S has proved to be the most popular version of the new EV, but when it comes to personalization, the sky’s the limit. “We see cars spec’d north of 300,000 pounds ($397,086),” said Walliser. “Individual content does not stop in case of an electric car. There have been some assumptions, and some people have been critical if people would be ready to do so.”

Based on the same underpinnings as the electric Porsche Cayenne, the Bentley Torcal is powered by a 113-kilowatt-hour battery that can be charged at up to 400 kilowatts. It can go from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes, and the estimated EPA range is expected to be over 300 miles.

Built on the Premium Platform Electric (PPE) architecture, it has two electric motors that make 810 horsepower and 881 pound-feet of torque in the standard Torcal and a whopping 876 hp and 996 lb-ft of torque in the Torcal S. When the model debuted in September, Bentley said it was the most powerful and quietest model to come out of the factory in Crewe.

To make the Torcal a reality, Bentley invested $463 million to upgrade its factory in England, plus at least the same amount for supply chain preparations and research and development, Walliser said.

Despite the electric SUV’s initial success, the British automaker is still heavily invested in gas and plug-in hybrid models, and the Bentayga isn’t going anywhere. “We have a very good combination with Torcal and Bentayga,” Walliser said. “The segment definitely has space for two cars.”

#4340. Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ new electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#4339. Gift Guide: 44 Cool, Fun, and Unique Gifts for Motorcyclists

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

We've tested and compiled an array of motorcycle gifts, gear, and accessories to help you find the right gifts for the motorcycle riders in your life.

This article was updated in November 2026.

The best motorcycle gifts don’t have to be flashy. A well-chosen upgrade can make a cold commute more comfortable, a long tour easier to manage, or time in the garage more rewarding. The trick is matching the present to the person: what they ride, where they go, and what gear they already own.

This guide covers a range of options, from protective apparel and useful electronics to compact accessories and garage staples. Whether you’re shopping for a longtime rider or someone still getting used to life on two wheels, you’ll find ideas for different styles, needs, and budgets.

Kriega is the leading brand in motorcycle baggage, and its backpacks are no different. Waterproof inside and with 20 liters of storage space, the R20 backpack is perfect for commuting and features Kreiga's harness-style fasteners. An innovative technology pioneered specifically for motorcycles, the chest clip and straps allow the bag's weight to be pushed forward, making sure that the weight stays centered on the back without disturbing your riding balance.

It's the perfect motorcycling backpack as far as we're concerned.

Give a motorcyclist a gift that makes every ride easier to relive—and can help document the unexpected. The Insta360 X5 Motorcycle Bundle captures 8K 360-degree video, letting riders choose angles later instead of fiddling with framing on the road. FlowState stabilization smooths bumpy footage, while the heavy-duty clamp and invisible selfie stick are ready for bike-mounted shots. It’s a fun way to share adventures and a useful record if a ride takes an unwelcome turn.

This extremely compact starter box is 33% thinner, 27% smaller, and 34% lighter than most portable jump-packs, so it slips right into your pocket. Rated at 1500 amps, it can even jump-start cars, motorcycles, trucks, ATVs, boats, RVs, vans, and SUVs. Best of all, it's equipped with a flashlight and two fast-charging USB ports, both A and C, so it can easily charge your favorite USB devices while it's in your pocket. No motorcyclist should flip up the kickstand without one.

This helmet wall mount is perfect for those who want to save space. It easily mounts on any wall and swivels to display helmets or other items as desired. When not in use, it can be pushed against the wall to take up less space. A bottom hook lets you hang your jacket, keeping all your riding gear together.

Hand signals from your riding buddy can only go so far, especially when a waving arm could mean anything. Communication systems go a long way toward enjoying group rides and Cardo's PackTalk PRO is the perfect communication system for individual and group use. The waterproof model includes a mesh network Bluetooth connection for phone calls, directions, and music while also allowing for rider-to-rider communications. JBL speakers are included in the package and make communications and music crystal clear. Best of all, you can set up voice commands and speed dial to make sure those eyes stay on the road.

Few gifts can improve a rider's safety as dramatically as the Brake Free Helmet Light. This clever wireless device mounts to the back of nearly any helmet and uses built-in sensors to detect braking, downshifting, and engine braking, illuminating bright LEDs at eye level for drivers behind you. With no wiring, no apps, and a weatherproof design, it's an easy upgrade that boosts visibility day or night. For riders who value safety without sacrificing simplicity, this is one of the smartest gifts on the road.

For the rider who owns the gloves, jacket, and boots, give them something that matters most when a ride goes wrong: Alpinestars’ Tech-Air 5 Plasma airbag system. This lightweight, breathable vest slips beneath a motorcycle jacket and deploys to protect the chest, ribs, back, and shoulders. It offers STREET, OFF-ROAD, and RACE modes, up to 30 hours of battery life, and a user-replaceable inflator. It’s an investment in safer miles—and a thoughtful gift with purpose. Available in sizes XS-4XL.

You don't need to be a biker to love this Lego set. It includes a two-speed gearbox and front and rear suspension for realistic movement. The attention to detail is impressive, like the turning handlebar and front and rear disc brakes. A kickstand, exhaust pipe, windshield, and dashboard add the little details that make this model true to the full-size version. Still, Lego enthusiasts who want a bigger challenge should try the 1900-piece Technic BMW M 1000 RR ($249.99 at Lego) set.

Quad Lock makes a huge variety of phone-mounting gear, and motorcyclist-specific products are some of the most popular. This particular unit, the Quad Lock Motorcycle Handlebar Mount, includes everything you'll need to install it on any motorcycle and allows for your choice of mounting angle. You'll also need to get one of QuadLock's sleek phone cases to complete the package.

#4338. REO Runabout T4X Is a Simple Truck Promising a $22K Starting Price

The single-cab T4X will be joined later by a crew-cab T4C and an S4C SUV, all promising the same blend of affordability and simplicity.

Affordable cars are gradually fading from the market as automakers chase profits over volume. Michigan-based Slate Auto wants to plug that gap with an electric truck set to enter production by the end of this year, but with a mere 205-mile range, the Slate Truck won’t fit everyone’s needs. That’s where REO Trucks aims to step in, promising a low-cost gas-powered pickup by late 2028.

REO Trucks revives the name of the company founded in 1905 by Ransom Eli Olds, after departing his first venture, Oldsmobile. The original REO, which went defunct in 1967, is best known for the Speed Wagon, an early ancestor to the modern pickup truck.

See all results for used cars for sale near 99224

So, it’s no surprise that the revived REO is launching with a pickup truck of its own. The Texas-based startup’s pitch is straightforward: pickup trucks have grown in size and cost, leaving the market without a compact, practical, affordable, and simple option. REO’s Runabout lineup is designed to fill that hole.

Three variants will be available, all sharing a common steel ladder-frame platform. The T4X is a two-door work truck, the T4C gains a crew cab, while the S4C is a family SUV. The bodies of all three models will be made from stamped steel, skipping aluminum or composites in an effort to reduce manufacturing and repair costs.

The clean, basic look was honed by frankstephenson design, the eponymous design house led by the man responsible for the McLaren P1 and 2001 Mini Cooper. REO says the confident stance was inspired by the American bison, with black plastic wheel arches protruding from the bodywork that REO says can be easily removed if customers want to fit larger tires.

The wide grille is flanked by rectangular LED headlights stacked one atop the other; below, there’s a chunky bumper with integrated tow hooks. The Runabout models have an upright cabin and flat, unadorned doors, with the handles mounted vertically on the pillars above. All three models are identical up to the B-pillar and have the same 119.6-inch wheelbase, and they all feature a rear bumper that integrates the taillights and a step.

The T4X will launch first, pairing a two-seat cab with a steel drop-side flatbed measuring 79.1 inches long and 70.6 inches wide. The tailgate includes a built-in ruler, cupholders, a bottle opener, and slots to hold phones and tablets. The T4C adds a pair of doors and a rear bench seat, with a 54.1-inch bed length. The S4C SUV, meanwhile, measures 182.7 inches long, about two inches shy of a Honda CR-V, and can seat six. It also features a one-piece, side-hinged tailgate and a rear window that can retract into the door.

See all results for used cars for sale near 99224

REO has yet to show the interior, which it says will be revealed in 2027, but REO promises plenty of physical controls, with buttons and switches designed to be operated while wearing gloves. Still, a digital gauge cluster will be present to display navigation and media. Unlike Slate, which cut costs with manual crank windows, REO is sticking with power windows. The Runabout will also get manually adjustable bucket seats, 120-volt power sockets, and a bit set in the glovebox that works for every fastener on the vehicle.

Under the hood will be a naturally aspirated four-cylinder engine, hooked up to a standard manual transmission. An automatic will be available, and all REOs will feature part-time four-wheel drive, with a mechanical transfer case with low-range ratios and a locking rear differential. REO says it’s targeting a powertrain life of 500,000 miles, avoiding turbochargers, direct injection, and a stop-start system in the name of longevity. The company didn’t reveal the engine’s capacity, nor where it will be sourced from.

REO keeps things simple with solid front and rear axles, suspended by coil springs up front and leaf springs at the rear. Braking is handled by ventilated front discs and rear drums, and the trucks feature hydraulic power steering. The steel wheels are wrapped in 245/70R-17 all-season tires.

A planned Ransom package will improve off-road capability, with 265/70R-17 all-terrain tires, upgraded dampers, and a 2.5-inch lift. The increased ride height raises the approach angle from 42.5 to 48.3 degrees and the breakover angle from 16.3 to 21.2 degrees. Ransom-equipped vehicles will be distinguished by orange dampers up front and upgraded leaf springs and dampers at the rear.

REO also wants to shake up the ownership experience, starting with a direct-to-consumer sales approach. REO promises its vehicles will be affordable and easy to maintain, making “right-to-repair” a core part of its mantra. REO will etch a service diagram under the hood, and REO says the bumpers, door panels, headliner, and trim are designed to be removable in under five minutes using common tools. The company also wants to provide open-source parts availability, with manufacturers that meet REO’s standard given factory mounting patterns and the ability to sell directly to customers via REO’s online marketplace.

The first T4X prototypes are set to be built in 2027, before full production starts in 2028, with deliveries kicking off later that year or early 2029. The T4X is supposed to start at just $21,500, with the T4C requiring $25,000 and the S4C coming in at $28,500. REO says production will come from an unnamed assembly plant in Texas and claims it already has 40,000 reservations, although that only requires paying a refundable $25 fee.

#4337. $20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the new NX7 in the comments, today.

#4336. BYD Is Winning Over Japan With A Very Japanese Kind Of EV

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BYD’s latest milestone in Japan would barely register on its sales charts back home in China. But selling 10,000 cars in a country dominated by domestic brands is progress, especially when part of that momentum comes from selling a vehicle tailored to what Japanese buyers actually want: a small, practical box on wheels, which also happens to be electric.

The Chinese automaker announced that its cumulative Japanese passenger-car sales had passed 10,000. Its first 5,000 took roughly two and a half years after deliveries began in January 2023. The next 5,000 took about 15 months. That includes its entire lineup, rather than just its newest and arguably most interesting addition: the Racco electric kei car.

It was bold to challenge Japan’s homegrown manufacturers with something designed specifically for their market and to create the world’s first kei car from a non-Japanese automaker. The Racco’s tall body, tiny footprint, and sliding rear doors follow the familiar Japanese formula for such vehicles. BYD didn’t need to reinvent anything, but its entry needed to be convincing.

Japanese buyers’ initial response to the Racco was encouraging. Launched on July 28, it attracted 1,002 orders in two weeks, the fastest order intake of any BYD model in Japan. By the end of August, that had grown to around 1,500. Roughly 80% of buyers chose the range-topping 300 Premium, clearly showing that the cheapest version was less attractive.

BYD credited the Racco with helping deliver record monthly orders across its Japanese lineup in August. Potential buyers who came to see the little EV ended up discovering its other models, too.

BYD offers six passenger-car models in Japan, and every one has a charging port. Five are fully electric: the Racco kei car, Dolphin hatchback, Seal sedan, Atto 3 crossover, and Sealion 7 SUV. The sixth, the Sealion 6 SUV, is a plug-in hybrid combining a gasoline engine with electric propulsion. That makes the entire lineup electrified, with no gasoline-only cars or conventional, non-plug-in hybrids on offer.

What’s more interesting is comparing the Racco’s sales performance to its main rival, the Nissan Sakura EV, which is also Japan’s best-selling electric car. In October, the Sakura EV sold 878 units, while the Racco sold 607. That’s almost 70% of the volume, marking a 37% rise over September.

The Nissan Sakura EV was Japan’s electric bestseller for a fourth consecutive year in 2025, but it could lose its crown to the Racco, which gives buyers more battery for less money, at least before subsidies. It starts at ¥2.145 million with a 22.4-kWh pack and 130 miles (210 kilometers) of WLTC range, while the Sakura starts at ¥2.449 million with a 20-kWh battery and 112 miles (180 km).

Even the longer-range Racco, with a 35.8-kWh pack capable of 199 miles (320 km), undercuts the entry-level Nissan at ¥2.398 million. The BYD also gets sliding rear doors instead of the Nissan’s conventional ones. What could help the Sakura stay ahead is the larger government subsidy it benefits from, which can make it cheaper to buy despite its higher sticker price.

It’s a tad early to call the Racco a Japanese sensation, but buyers are clearly interested. This newcomer is already selling roughly seven cars for every ten Sakuras in one month, so it definitely deserves attention.

#4334. China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

#4333. Chevy, GMC, and Cadillac EV Owners Can Now Plug And Charge At Electrify America

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The ability to simply plug in at a fast-charging station and start charging within seconds was once a luxury once reserved for Tesla drivers at Superchargers. However, with the advent of Plug & Charge, this seamless operation has come to many other brands, including General Motors. GM announced Plug & Charge support back in 2022, starting with EVGo. Now, Plug & Charge is all in one space via GM's Energy Pass App, with Ionna and ChargePoint added to the Plug & Charge list in 2026. Today, it confirmed support for the largest CCS fast-charging network in the country: Electrify America.

The update comes to CCS-equipped General Motors EVs, with NACS-equipped EVs to follow in early 2027.

To use Plug & Charge with Electrify America (or any other charging network that has a Plug & Charge agreement with GM), the driver must be registered with GM’s Energy Pass in the MyChevrolet, MyGMC, or MyCadillac app. The Energy Pass links your EV with a default payment type, allowing charging stations to start the charging event and bill the driver directly without navigating any other app. The driver doesn’t have to do anything but plug in; there’s no need to use a third-party app or fiddle around with a frustrating interface on the charger itself.

The function works with Ionna, EVGo, and ChargePoint, and now Electrify America. The Energy Pass section of the apps not only controls payment, but serves as a one-stop-shop by showing past charging history and letting you locate and navigate to charging stations. Tesla Supercharging Plug & Charge was announced in summer 2026, but it has not quite yet come to the Energy Pass app yet. It should arrive in 2027.

In order to get more people behind the wheel of EVs, industry leaders have stressed that the ease and quality of charging stops must improve. This goes beyond just making sure there are enough charging stations available and making sure they’re in working order. From start to finish, the charging experience should be easy and painless. Saving time and making things as seamless as possible should help make the charging experience nearly frictionless, which is a good thing for EV adoption.

“Bringing that experience to GM EV drivers is another important step forward. It removes friction from the charging experience and lets customers focus on what matters: plugging in, charging, and getting back on the road.” Robert Barrosa, president and CEO of Electrify America, said in a press release.

GM says that on average, the flow of power should start within 45 seconds of plugging in. That is significantly quicker and easier than navigating through a series of menus and apps to start a charging event without Plug & Charge.

Importantly, the addition of Electrify America brings 6,200 chargers that are capable of speeds of up to 350 kW. Some of GM’s largest EVs, like the Chevrolet Silverado EV or Cadillac Escalade IQ, advertise their charging times when connected these ultra-fast charger.

Participation in GM Energy Pass is optional. If the driver doesn’t want to use it, they are free to use the existing charging station apps to charge the vehicle. But it should be easier to use Energy Pass, at least at Electrify America, EVGo, and Ionna stations.

#4331. A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

A promising new approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

"We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic."

The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.

Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

Applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.

How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer

To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

The researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.

That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.

Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.

But the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

This discovery could be particularly important for developing faster and more compact computer components.

"Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout."

In other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.

The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.

A New Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing

As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly important goal.

Caretta believes the new findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

It also shows that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta said. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us."

The research received funding from the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

#4330. High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

The ES is offered only in ES350h hybrid guise. Front-wheel-drive models are powered by a hybrid powertrain consisting of a 2.5-liter four-cylinder and two electric motors that combine for 244 horsepower. A continuously variable automatic transmission is standard. All-wheel drive models get a third electric motor that powers the rear axle, but combined horsepower remains the same at 244 horsepower.

The ES has always been a smooth operator, and this generation is no different. Lexus says this new model has more chassis rigidity than older models, and more attention has been spent on reducing body vibrations. When we drove the ES350h, we were impressed by its ride quality, but noted that it's no sports sedan, as its handling is still easy-going rather than sharp-edged.

In Comparison: The ES350h is quicker than as the similarly sized Toyota Crown, which needed 7.2 seconds to hit 60 mph at our test track.

The EPA rates the ES hybrid as high as 48 mpg city, 44 mpg highway, and 46 mpg combined. The all-wheel-drive version is slightly less efficient, with ratings of 47 mpg city, 42 mpg highway, and 44 mpg combined. On our real-world 75-mph highway fuel economy route, the all-wheel-drive ES350h matched its EPA rating, delivering 42 mpg. For more information about the ES's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

First Row: With its stylish dash and high-quality cabin materials, the ES creates a plush environment for passengers. Ambient interior lighting and 3D-printed faux bamboo wood trim are used on the door panels for an upscale look. The seats are comfortable, and there's plenty of space for adults of all sizes to find their ideal driving position.

Second Row: A pair of passengers will also have no issues settling into the ES's comfortable back seat. Upscale environs await you in the rear compartment, with nicely cushioned seats and dedicated rear-seat air vents for the climate control.

Cargo Capacity: A large trunk gives the ES ample cargo space, and we expect to find it similarly sized to rivals. When we get a chance, we'll stuff the trunk with carry-on suitcases and report our findings here.

A 14.0-inch infotainment touchscreen takes a prominent location on the ES's dashboard. It features wireless connectivity for smartphones with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, as well as native navigation. A 10-speaker stereo is standard, and a 17-speaker Mark Levinson premium stereo system is available as an option.

A host of driver-assistance features comes standard, including adaptive cruise control, blind-spot monitoring, and automatic high-beam headlamps.

For information about the ES's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

Lexus provides longer warranty coverage than BMW and Mercedes-Benz. However, it trails Genesis, which offers one of the best warranties in the segment.

#4328. Mowing milestone: Greenzie surpasses 255,000 autonomous miles mowed

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie announced the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The company says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

#4327. Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors

Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

#4326. REO Runabout vs. Slate Truck: Which Sub-$30,000 Truck Is Better?

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Like the idea of a Slate but don't want an EV? Well, an upstart from Dallas, Texas has just the thing for you. That is, if it ever becomes a reality. Startup company REO recently unveiled renderings of its new truck, dubbed the Runabout. It's a similar idea to Slate, with just one basic frame, three different body variants to choose from, no frills, a bunch of customization, and a sub-$30,000 price tag. The main difference is that that Runabout uses a four-cylinder gas engine, rather than electric motors. So how does it compare to Slate?

First, let's look at price. The most basic Slate you can get—cheekily called "The Blank Slate"—costs $24,950, and it's a two-door pickup with nothing more than some seats, a steering wheel, a battery, and a single rear electric motor to get you around. There's no radio, power windows, or screens to speak of.

The cheapest REO you can get will be the Runabout T4X, which costs $21,500*. Note the asterisk, as REO says the current listed price is an estimate, and the company has no factory or clear plans for getting it to market. For that shockingly low price, it's estimated that you'll get a four-cylinder engine, a choice of either a six-speed manual or automatic transmission, and mechanical four-wheel drive. It's a two-door, two-seat pickup with drop-down sides for the bed, like a Kei truck.

What four-cylinder engine will the Runabout have and which manufacturer will supply it? REO isn't saying. There are far more questions than answers so far. REO does say that it has a "targeted powertrain life of 500,000 miles." To quote myself reading that in the press release: "lol."

While Slate uses a hybrid body-on-frame style chassis, the REO has an old-school ladder frame, like a classic pickup. It's similar to slate in that it offers modular body styles, but with key differences. There's a two-door pickup and an SUV version, like Slate, but there's also a four-door pickup, which Slate doesn't have. REO claims its truck has solid rear axles, too, to give it more off-road credibility.

The design isn't bad, even if it looks like a Grand Theft Auto version of an Australian-market Land Cruiser, but that's to be expected. REO hired longtime automotive designer Frank Stephenson, whose previous work includes the first BMW-owned Mini Cooper, the Maserati MC12, and the McLaren P1. Overall, it looks handsome enough and utilitarian, even if all the photos are just renders at this point.

Inside, REO's truck is said to be pretty barebones (it hasn't been revealed yet), but not as barebones as Slate's. There's a digital screen for gauges and one for navigation, but everything else has a physical control. You're probably wondering if it has power or hand-crank windows. REO used its press release to throw a little shade: " Each model will feature power windows for convenience: hand-cranks are best left to others."

The entire idea behind REO is to offer the sort of basic pickups customers loved in the '80s and '90s, trucks that were simple utilitarian workhorses and nothing else. It's an admirable goal, especially given how expensive pickups have become. But do customers want to go backward in powertrain technology, especially with affordable mainstream electric trucks like the Ford Fathom coming to market soon?

So for less money, you can get a potentially more capable truck, in a similar configuration as the Slate, with a bit of extra interior comfort. But you lose the electric powertrain, which reduces maintenance and fuel costs. Instead, you'll have to make due with a generic four-cylinder of some sort. There is one big "if," though. You can only buy one if REO ever actually makes it. Sure, having a design by Frank Stephenson helps it feel more real, but just because they found the money to pay him to design something doesn't mean they'll actually get around to building it.

Slate is already here, it's ready to launch production vehicles soon. We've seen them in person, touched them, and tested them. Until REO can actually muster a viable product, it should probably avoid throwing anymore shade in its press releases.

#4325. Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a new video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”

On Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

As we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

So Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

The memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

That’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

#4324. Volkswagen prices its new ID. Cross for the UK, but the $35,000 version comes later

Volkswagen revealed how much its new ID. Cross will cost, with prices starting at around $35,000 in the UK. But if you’re hoping to get the cheaper version, you’ll have to wait a bit longer.

After opening orders for the ID. Cross in Europe in July, Volkswagen is preparing to launch the entry-level electric SUV in the UK.

The ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.

Following the ID. Polo, the ID. Cross is the latest from Volkswagen’s electric urban family of compact cars.

The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.

When the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.

Like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.

The ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.

With DC fast charging of up to 105 and 88 kW, Volkswagen said the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in as little as 23 minutes.

All versions are equipped with vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, allowing it to be used as a mobile power bank for an e-bike, campsite, or other external electronic devices.

Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit Pro instrument display and a 12.9″ infotainment screen. Based on driver feedback, Volkswagen brought back physical buttons for climate control and other vehicle functions.

Volkswagen will open orders for the ID. Cross Life and Style trims in the UK with the 52 kWh battery and 208 hp (211 PS) motor will go on sale on Thursday, November 19, starting at £30,260 ($40,000) and £33,675 ($44,500), respectively.

The base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).

Volkswagen said the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.

In Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.

As the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”

Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the new ID. Tiguan, which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.

#4323. Mercedes Is Officially Bringing Back the Benz-Branded SL Roadster

The new Mercedes-Benz SL-class will launch sometime next year as part of a broader mid-cycle refresh.

The swanky SL-class will once again wear a Mercedes-Benz, according to the company’s CEO Ola Källenius. He reportedly told Autocar that the Benz-branded roadster was resurrected based on buyer feedback about the current seventh-generation SL. The GT will remain a performance-focused machine for those looking for sportier handling, but the new Mercedes-Benz SL will take more of a Sunday-driver approach, favoring comfort and ride quality over pure power. The two models will still share drivetrains, platforms, and other features, and they’ll both get revised engines to meet new emissions regulations in Europe.
