#4322. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

"GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens."

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies

The research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, said the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association."

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant."

Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs."

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs."

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy."

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

#4321. Rivian Is Inviting Owners To Beta Test Its New Point-To-Point Assisted Driving Tech

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Rivian started gauging interest for its Autonomy Early Access Program last month. They asked owners to let the company know if they were interested in being one of the first drivers to get their hands on its point-to-point driving software. This week, it will begin reviewing those applicants and, if chosen, owners will be welcomed into the Early Access beta—with one catch.

The automaker updated its website recently to outline the requirements it will use to decide whether or not to grant access to the program. It turns out that it's not as easy as just clicking an "I Agree" button or paying for some sort of subscription. Rivian actually has a strict set of requirements that it uses to pick its testers.

For starters, Rivian is only accepting applicants from either California or Florida. That's expected to change later, but for now, Rivian says that owners outside of these states can express their interest so it can decide where to expand the program later on.

Then there are the vehicle requirements. Owners must have one of the automaker's new Rivian R2 electric SUVs, or an R1 vehicle on its Gen 2 platform (sorry, Gen 1 owners). You also need a paid Autonomy+ subscription, and Rivian will consider how frequently you use its existing autonomy features while driving.

You also have to be a safe driver. Rivian says it will review your driving safety score, which evaluates in-car events like forward collision warnings, true collision events, and "other safety-related metrics." RivianTrackr says that the program terms state that the automaker may also look into your driving history to determine if it is free from "DUI, reckless driving, license suspension, major moving violations or at-fault accidents."

Rivian's own terms note that to remain eligible and enrolled, participants will be expected to use the point-to-point features weekly, provide feedback via surveys, log issues (if they arise), and share certain data under a Non-Disclosure Agreement. RivianTrackr says the agreement includes location and camera data.

The entire idea behind the Early Access Program is to focus on Rivian's Point to Point autonomy, a Rivian spokesperson confirmed to InsideEVs. And while it doesn't have a deadline for how many folks it will enroll in the program (or how long the program will last), Rivian says it plans to scale it rapidly and make the features available for new vehicle test drives at a later date.

While most of the program details and point-to-point features are tight-lipped as of now, it likely won't be long before we get to hear some of the juicy details. Rivian's AI & Autonomy Day is coming up fast on December 9th, which Rivian says is "all about" Autonomy+.

So if you're an onlooker, you may have to wait another three weeks before some key details are shared. But if you're an owner who happens to meet all of the criteria to join the Early Access Program, Rivian says you can register your interest via your Rivian account for a chance to be selected to join.

#4320. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

#4319. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

Tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

#4318. Over 1 Million Hondas Are Being Investigated for Start-Stop Failures

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has gotten hundreds of complaints that engines are not restarting after coming to a stop at traffic lights.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has launched an investigation into Honda’s automatic engine start-stop system. The inquiry comes after NHTSA received hundreds of complaints, with owners stating that their engines were failing to automatically restart after coming to a full stop at a traffic light.

The investigation was announced on Friday, November 13, and covers 1,033,632 total vehicles. The affected models are the Honda Passport, Odyssey, Pilot, and Ridgeline, along with the Acura MDX, all from between the 2024 and 2026 model years.

See all results for new 2026 Honda Passport for sale near 94043

In total, NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation has been sent 701 complaints about the automatic start-stop feature. The system is supposed to automatically turn off the engine when the vehicle comes to a complete stop, and it’s supposed to automatically restart the engine when the driver takes their foot off the brake pedal. However, “the complaints allege that the engines are failing to restart once they have been shut off by this system.” NHTSA says that there have been no injuries related to the stop-start system problems.

This isn’t the first time that this issue has arisen with Honda’s automatic start-stop system, which is meant to improve fuel economy by limiting idle time. In 2025, the federal government investigated the system, looking at 2.2 million units of the Pilot, Odyssey, Passport, Ridgeline, MDX, and Acura TLX. The previous investigation covered all of the vehicles in the current investigation, except for the 2026 model year.

Although the system failure is similar in both populations, “the vehicles in this current investigation appear to have different root causes and respond differently to repairs,” NHTSA says. More information should continue to emerge as NHTSA continues its investigation.

#4317. Hyundai IONIQ 5 caught with a new high-tech interior and big display screen

Hyundai appears to be testing a new high-tech setup in the IONIQ 5. A prototype was spotted with the door wide open, exposing a large display and a layout that looks very different from the current model.

Is the IONIQ 5 next in line for an overhaul? Another mysterious IONIQ 5 test mule was recently caught in a parking garage in South Korea, revealing what’s rumored to be Hyundai’s software-defined vehicle (SDV).

Hyundai is betting heavily on software, AI, autonomous driving, robotics, and more as it expands from a traditional auto manufacturer to a “software-centric mobility leader.”

At the heart of it all is Hyundai Motor Group’s new Pleos Connect, an advanced in-vehicle infotainment and software platform.

Built on Android Automotive OS, Hyundai’s new setup features a larger, tablet-style infotainment screen with apps, split-screen views, and more. It’s similar to using a smartphone with an easier-to-use, customizable layout.

The Grandeur was the first to launch with Hyundai’s Pleos in Korea in May, followed by the IONIQ 3 in Europe. In the US, the new Tucson will be the first to go on sale with Pleos in early 2027.

Is the IONIQ 5 next in line? Hyundai aims to launch its first SDV as early as next year, and the IONIQ 5 appears to be a contender.

An IONIQ 5 test car was captured again (shown below) by @JHS_spyshot_official in a Korean parking garage, but this time the door was wide open, offering a clear view of the new setup.

A post shared by JHS (@jhs_spyshot_official)

Hyundai appeared to be testing automated parking features, and as you can see, the setup is considerably different from the current IONIQ 5.

A large infotainment display sits at the center that appears to be running Hyundai Pleos, instead of the current dual 12.3″ screens. Meanwhile, the steering wheel and dash both appear to be completely redesigned.

Although it’s hard to see, previous spy images show the IONIQ 5 SDV test car with no driver display, with all information expected to move to the large center infotainment screen.

By 2030, Hyundai Motor Group plans to equip around 20 million Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis vehicles with the new Pleos setup.

Over the summer, an IONIQ 6 prototype was spotted near Hyundai’s R&D hub in Europe with a similar high-tech setup.

With Hyundai planning to launch its first SDV as early as next year, we should learn more soon.

#4316. M3 Goes EV! We Drive a Prototype as the M Car Undergoes a Monumental Change

With four motors making around 838 horsepower, the 2027 BMW M3 prototype is a monster on the track.

Most BMW fans cannot help falling all over themselves when a new M3 is launched, but this time they might get well and truly tripped up. That’s because what BMW is calling “the fastest and most powerful BMW M3 of all time” is 100 percent electric. There’s no mention of a gasoline version and no special EV designation tagged onto the name, just “here’s the new 2027 BMW M3, and we hope you like it,” or words to that effect.

After driving a camouflaged prototype and hearing all the dirty details at BMW’s Miramas test center in southern France, we most certainly do.

This machine has four electrically excited synchronous motors, one for each wheel. The pair at each axle is not quite what you expect, with one motor situated ahead of the other and a reduction gear for one of them on each side of the shared housing. The front-axle motors make approximately 644 horsepower and 398 pound-feet of torque, while the pair on the rear axle is good for about 751 horsepower and 738 pound-feet. Combined output is likewise still subject to an asterisk at this pre-production stage, but total power is at least 838 horsepower, and torque is an axle-twisting 885 pound-feet. If you’re thinking the sum total is less than the two axles, you are absolutely correct. The surplus is there to allow for serious torque vectoring, both front to rear and side to side. In normal driving, the car operates strictly in rear-wheel drive, with the front axle brought in whenever there’s acceleration, if the situation demands front-axle recuperation, or if you have the drivetrain set to Sport mode.

See all results for new 2028 BMW M3 EV for sale near 60440

Four motors require precise and rapid control during acceleration and braking, but they also play an outsize role in cornering. It all operates much more smoothly and immediately than any electronically controlled differential or transfer case ever could, so you absolutely get what you request. The so-called Heart of Joy (essentially another name for the M Dynamic Performance Control module) is the single ECU that oversees everything in the powertrain and driving dynamics arena. It’s the brain that seamlessly decides what motor is required for whatever demands you place on the car by looking at steering position, accelerator input, and braking demands, with a nod toward the basic settings that you have dialed in.

The battery that powers all of this is specific to the M3, even though it fits in a similarly sized case as the one in the i3. It’s designed to give higher peak and sustained power output and is capable of higher energy recuperation (up to 540 kilowatts) and faster charging (420 kilowatts), which means it has a higher level of cooling. The battery capacity is slightly lower for all this, currently sitting at about 100 kWh. Estimated EPA range is currently 300 miles or so, but all of these numbers are subject to change. As for the difference between how this battery pack is installed versus the i3’s, the M3 gains a direct connection to the front and rear axle subframes for enhanced torsional rigidity for more precise handling.

See all results for new 2028 BMW M3 EV for sale near 60440

Whatever the underlying mumbo jumbo, we can say that it really works, and the result is simply epic. We first went out in the default mode, with the drivetrain, chassis, steering, and brakes set to Comfort and energy recovery set to Mid, just to get a feel of the track. Once we knew where we were going, we let fly with the M1 button, and that brought everything to Sport mode but left the energy recovery in Mid and, crucially, left the DSC stability control setting in On. We pressed the car hard, and the M3 absolutely responded, and our pace built immensely. But that eventually resulted in a bit too much understeer as speeds climbed, which led to a brief off-track excursion, as they say in the business. We kept on going, but the car was imposing a limit on our fun.

We did what you would do at that point and duly selected the M2 button. That setting was programmed by our hosts to bring the drivetrain and chassis up to Sport+ and raised the recuperation to Max. It also put the DSC in a more permissive state, otherwise known as MDM, and all of that was the magic bullet. The car now dived toward apexes and slithered nicely out of corners. The front end was quite pointy, and the rear now had permission to loosen up. Our lap times fell, and our grin widened. This car felt alive. It really did feel like an M3, just like no other before it. Through it all, the braking response felt entirely natural, probably because on the track there was a strong base level of recuperation, overlaid with a thin veneer of friction braking for a precise feel of what is happening underfoot.

Interestingly, there is a sound accompanying all of this, although BMW says it’s not modeled on any particular car. We drove it with the eDrive set to Auto, which delivers the augmented sound of six gears known as “stages.” You don’t have to shift in this mode, and there’s no real interruption of power, but the interior sound level rises and falls as the car progresses up and down through each stage. There’s extra emphasis on powertrain load and aggression, too, so when you’re driving the M3 hard, it really does give you the auditory cues that you miss when you drive an otherwise-quiet EV. If you want a manual-like experience, you can set the eDrive accordingly, and then you’ll get shift lights, and it’ll even cut power if you don’t upshift at the right time. In the time we had, this setting was not particularly fun. We’ll table this issue for now, probably until we can get our own M3 to soak in. You can also turn the eDrive to Off, in which setting the car will just quietly amble along like any other EV, but what’s the fun in that?

The prototype’s camouflage didn’t do much to cover up the exterior of the new M3, as it was formfitting. That said, you couldn’t really get a sense of the exterior look of the car, although it was still clear that every panel below the greenhouse was different from the i3. The body is distinctly pulled out to cover the wide Michelin Pilot Sport S 6 tires. Also clear to see were the M Yellow DRLs and the track lights below them, as well as many of the carbon-fiber bits, such as the hood vents, the rockers, and the mirror housings.

It was even more difficult to see what was going on inside, as much of the interior was obscured. But you could still see some things, such as the steering wheel and its extra buttons. The top of the “wings” (because the spokes are lower down in typical Neue Klasse parlance) has two extra red buttons per side. There are the M1 and M2 buttons, but there’s also the M Setup button you use in conjunction with the touchscreen to program each one. The fourth button is interesting; press it twice to deactivate the ADAS active-safety minders. For track work, it’s nice to have one button that will do all that. The 17.9-inch central screen was obvious, but BMW had it covered much of the time, except to show the new screens that had to do with setting up the M buttons. The Panoramic Vision screen at the base of the windshield was mostly visible and mostly the same apart from fonts and the like, but for some reason the central section was blocked off.

As for what it’s called, the car’s official name is just 2027 BMW M3. Like we said, there’s no EV or Electric nomenclature tagged onto the end. As for the unofficial model code that you may be wondering about, that is ZA0. More will be divulged as we get closer to its summer 2027 launch date, including the price. We have a $90,000 placeholder, but that is subject to change. As for an ICE version, there is no official word from BMW. Stay tuned.

#4315. AI supercharges laser physics with a stunning 250x speed boost

Simulating the complex behavior of light inside powerful laser systems requires enormous computing resources, making it difficult for researchers to predict and adjust laser performance quickly. Now, scientists at Stanford University, the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), and SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have developed an artificial intelligence model that dramatically accelerates these calculations. Using deep learning, the new approach reproduces the results of conventional simulations in a fraction of the time while maintaining high accuracy across a wide variety of laser pulse shapes.

The advance focuses on a branch of physics called second-order nonlinear optics, also known as χ2 processes. These interactions occur when light waves exchange energy while traveling through specially designed crystals, allowing scientists to change the frequency of light and precisely control the shape of laser pulses. Such capabilities are particularly important at large scientific facilities that use lasers to generate intense X-rays.

How Laser Light Helps Generate Powerful X-Rays

At SLAC's upgraded Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS-II), laser pulses undergo a series of transformations before they can help produce X-rays. Infrared light is first converted into green light and then into ultraviolet (UV) light. The resulting UV pulse strikes a cathode, releasing a cluster of electrons that is accelerated and manipulated to generate powerful X-ray pulses.

The precise timing and shape of the UV pulse help determine the characteristics of the electron bunch. Those characteristics, in turn, influence the quality of the X-rays that researchers use in scientific experiments. Accurately predicting the conversion of light between different frequencies is therefore an important part of optimizing the system.

The new AI approach, described in the journal Advanced Photonics, was developed specifically to model the nonlinear χ2 interactions involved in this frequency conversion process.

AI Replaces Time-Consuming Laser Calculations

Traditionally, scientists simulate these interactions by solving a complex mathematical equation known as the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. A widely used technique called the split-step Fourier method (SSFM) calculates how light changes as it travels through a material, repeatedly switching between representations of the pulse in time and frequency.

Although the method produces accurate results, it demands substantial computing power. In the complete laser simulation examined by the researchers, this calculation alone accounts for approximately 95 percent of the total processing time.

To overcome that bottleneck, the team developed an AI model based on a type of recurrent neural network called LSTM (long short-term memory). Building on earlier research that used similar networks to predict how laser pulses travel through optical fibers, the scientists adapted the approach to handle more complicated interactions involving multiple light waves.

They tested the model using a process called noncollinear sum frequency generation, or SFG, in which three interconnected light fields evolve together inside a crystal. The simulations covered a wide variety of laser pulse shapes, providing a demanding test of the model's ability to reproduce complex optical behavior.

One important innovation was the way the AI handles information. Rather than repeatedly converting calculations between time and frequency, as conventional simulations do, the neural network works entirely with a compressed representation of the light's frequency characteristics. This eliminates much of the repetitive computation that makes traditional methods slow.

Complex Laser Simulations in Just Milliseconds

The results showed that the AI model could accurately recreate how laser pulses change over time and across different frequencies, even under particularly challenging conditions. These included pulses with pronounced gaps in their frequency spectra and strong variations in optical phase.

When the researchers processed multiple simulations together using graphics processing units, the average calculation time for each simulation dropped to just a few milliseconds. That represents an improvement of orders of magnitude over conventional methods, making it possible to obtain predictions far more quickly without substantially compromising accuracy.

The system also demonstrated an important ability to capture the interconnected behavior of the light waves. When the AI accurately predicted the main output of the SFG process, its predictions for the other interacting fields were generally accurate as well. This suggests that the network learned important features of the overall interaction rather than simply reproducing one output.

Toward Smarter Lasers and Real-Time Control

Beyond faster simulations, the researchers envision connecting AI models directly to operating laser systems. Their approach uses a modular design in which individual physical processes can be represented by separate trained neural networks. Combining these models could make it possible to predict the behavior of an entire experimental system while it is running.

One potential application is the creation of digital twins, detailed virtual models that mirror the behavior of real laser equipment. With sufficiently fast and accurate predictions, these systems could help researchers monitor experiments, anticipate changes, and adjust laser settings in response to changing conditions.

The technology could also support adaptive laser control and closer integration with diagnostic instruments that measure the results of experiments. By removing a major computational obstacle, the research brings the possibility of more responsive, precisely controlled laser systems closer to reality, with potential benefits for a wide range of scientific facilities that rely on powerful lasers.

#4314. Trump again orders broken coal plant to stay open, even after court said it’s illegal

The Department of Energy has issued a seventh “emergency” order forcing J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan to remain open, 534 days after the plant’s planned retirement. The orders have cost ratepayers $303 million and counting, causing electricity prices to increase amid a global energy crisis.

One of the Department of Energy’s recent tactics has been to issue “emergency orders” forcing coal plants to stay open, even when nobody wants them open.

The DoE has used this on six coal plants (and one oil-and-gas plant) in six states, claiming that the plants need to be kept open for “reliability.”

The problem, of course, is that coal is the least reliable form of energy we have available to us. It’s also expensive and polluting, which is why coal use has been plummeting in recent years, dropping from a high of around half of US electricity generation in the early 2000s, down to 17% now.

So everyone is trying to get off coal, for good reason. And when I say “everyone,” I mean everyone – even the owners of the plants subject to these orders have made filings opposing the orders.

The only person trying to keep these coal plants open is fossil shill Chris Wright, posing as head of the Department of Energy, whose main goal is to make American energy supply more expensive and less secure, and ensure that Americans suffer as much harm as possible from it, both to their lungs and pocketbooks.

Each of these orders was obviously illegal from the start – there is no emergency that should force broken coal plants to be reopened, at great cost, in order to sit there idle, providing nothing for ratepayers in the region who are on the hook for the hundreds of millions of dollars that these orders will cost.

Thankfully, courts agreed – even if it took them a while. After more than a year of this nonsense, a federal appeals court blocked these “emergency orders,” specifically targeting the order for the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan. The court unanimously found that there was no emergency keeping it open.

The orders for the other plants are all subject to similar lawsuits, and given the ruling for the Campbell plant, it is expected that courts will find similarly for each of them.

However, despite that order, the DoE has continued its illegal actions. Today, it issued another 90-day “emergency order” forcing the Campbell plant to stay open until mid-February. It does this as it requests a re-hearing on the previous decision, which was unanimously found to be illegal.

In the interim, Americans have dealt with skyrocketing energy prices throughout all aspects of life, largely driven by a now 8+ month long war of choice in Iran. This war was started by an ignoramus posing as president who cannot legally hold office in the US, and who was recently widely rebuked by the American public, largely due to his illegal actions to raise their energy prices.

That rebuke wasn’t enough to stop the fossil shills squatting in the White House though, if today’s actions are any indication. The 90 day order will continue to balloon costs, keeping a coal plant open that nobody wants open, even its own operators who had already planned for its retirement.

Who knew that MAGA meant battling the well-documented improvements of modernity, like clean(er) and cheaper energy, vaccines, scientific R&D, etc.?

In a recent filing, the plants owners said “From the date the first emergency order became effective through September 30, 2026, the amount Consumers expects to seek recovery from FERC associated with the emergency orders, including amounts already requested, is $303 million.”

This amount is in addition to the hundreds of millions of dollars of costs incurred by the other six plants subject to these false emergency orders, bringing costs up by over $600 million across the country just from these emergency orders alone. The Campbell plant is the worst of the bunch in terms of pollution – which isn’t accounted for in the $600 million number, meaning American health costs are rising even more in addition to the staffing costs for these broken plants.

In addition, the DoE has channeled nearly a billion dollars in additional subsidies to this dead form of electricity generation, doing so after coal industry lobbyists asked them for these specific emergency orders. #4313. Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

Tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The company confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a new production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:

If you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we announced a first investment of around € 3b in a new manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the new production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla plans to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company says it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”

It leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the new hall will be bigger than the original factory.

The building isn’t new. Tesla laid out a plan to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the new hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

The EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

The Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU said no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

And the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

This is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

#4311. BYD is bringing its $10,000 ‘Great’ Seagull overseas, but it won’t replace the Dolphin Surf

BYD’s new, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

In China, the new Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

The second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s new Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the new version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

Inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The new setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

The optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

In China, BYD offers the new Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

The current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

#4310. Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises important questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

"Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," said Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals."

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal

The next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

The study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

However, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

In this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

Approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments showed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

"We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a new avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward new strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

#4309. Arc Raiders just keeps breaking its own Steam player records

Word of mouth has done wonders for the popularity of Arc Raiders, clearly more than all the pre-launch marketing and hype.

Arc Raiders just cannot be stopped. The extraction shooter from Embark Studios has once again attracted more players over the weekend than it has in its launch week, and over its first weekend on the market.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

The day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

That figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

To everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside new Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. And, if you just jumped in over the weekend, you’re definitely going to find these Arc Raiders tips very helpful.

#4308. Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and says it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

At 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

The SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

FHP said the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

This record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it says Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

So Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

Autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

There’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

This is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a new record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

This is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

Tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

We’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

#4306. Aston Martin and Fernando Alonso Will Take on the 2027 Dakar Rally

Known for elegant road cars, Aston is gearing up for its first rally-raid competition, working with Prodrive on the radical Dreadnought racer.

The name Aston Martin conjures images of luxurious grand tourers flowing swiftly down curving mountain roads, perhaps with a certain British MI6 secret agent sitting suavely behind the wheel. In recent years, Aston Martin has also become increasingly involved in racing, from its Vantage-based GT3 car to Formula 1. Now, the British automaker is embarking on a new motorsports challenge, and it’s not one we were expecting: Aston Martin will compete in the 2027 Dakar Rally.

Dakar, for those unfamiliar, is one of the most grueling off-road rally races in the world. Starting in 1979, drivers originally raced from Paris, France, to Dakar, Senegal. More recently, the rally has been held in the desert of Saudi Arabia, departing its original location after violence in Mauritania. Now, the tension in the Middle East caused by the war between the United States and Iran has forced the Dakar Rally to move once again.

See all results for used Aston Martin for sale near 48105

Aston Martin’s first Dakar will see the fledgling outfit run from Loulé, Portugal, to Marrakesh, Morocco. Although this is Aston Martin’s first time entering the Dakar Rally, it has found a well-versed partner in Prodrive. The British racing and engineering company developed the BRX Hunter, which ran from 2021 to 2024, managing a best finish of second, before partnering with Dacia to create the Sandrider, which ran in 2025 and 2026, triumphing at last year’s event.

Prodrive and Aston Martin already work together on endurance GT racing, so it’s not a shock that Aston Martin collaborated with Prodrive to develop and build the new Dreadnought rally raid car. This rally challenger borrows its name from an SUV designed by Aston Martin for the recently launched Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 video game, and it shares some design elements with the virtual off-roader.

The front end is characterized by a pair of octagonal lights that mirror the square pixel lighting from the video-game SUV. Like the Sandrider, the spare tires are tucked into the bodywork just behind the rear doors. Around back, the slatted roof, tall ducktail spoiler, and intricate LED lighting carry over from the Call of Duty Dreadnought. No technical details were revealed about the Dakar racer just yet, but we wouldn’t be surprised if the Aston Martin shares some components with the Sandrider, just as it was an evolution of the BRX Hunter. A new engine is likely—the Hunter used a Ford twin-turbo 3.5-liter V-6 and the Dacia used a Nissan twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6—but we don’t know what Aston Martin and Prodrive settled on, although a Mercedes-Benz V-6 seems likely.

See all results for used Aston Martin for sale near 48105

Aston Martin has also amassed an incredible lineup of drivers for the race. Two-time Formula 1 World Champion and current Aston Martin F1 driver Fernando Alonso will take a break from driving on pavement to pilot one of the three Dreadnoughts. Alonso has competed in the Dakar Rally once before, taking a Toyota Hilux race truck to 13th place in 2020.

The second car will be driven by Sébastien Loeb, a nine-time World Rally champion who has finished second three times at the Dakar. Loeb is extremely familiar with Prodrive machinery, spending the last six years driving the BRX Hunter and the Dacia Sandrider. Last but not least, Aston Martin has signed Lucas Moraes, the 2025 World Rally Raid champion who has a best finish at Dakar of third, to drive the third Dreadnought.

The 2027 Dakar Rally kicks off on January 9 and runs over 12 stages until January 23. The competitors will cover a total of 4228 miles, with 2600 miles consisting of special stages, the timed portion of the event that occurs over the most challenging terrain. While Aston Martin will be a fresh face in the Dakar bivouac, a seasoned group of drivers and a successful partner in Prodrive give the new team promise when the rally kicks off in two months.
